---
title: "Association Between Body Mass and Species"
---

```{python}
#| echo: false
import itertools

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

np.random.seed(206) # used by jitter parameter in one of our plots

penguins = pd.read_csv("penguins.csv").dropna()
```

## The Regression Model

We fit a regression model using all categorical variables:

$$
\text{Body Mass (g)} = \beta_{0}
+ \text{Is Male} \times \beta_{1}
+ \text{Is Chinstrap} \times \beta_{2}
+ \text{Is Gentoo} \times \beta_{3}
$$

- Here $\beta_{0}$ is the average body mass of a female Adelie penguin. This is the reference group.
- The coefficient $\beta_{1}$ captures the mean shift due to being a male penguin.
- The coefficient $\beta_{2}$ captures the mean shift due to being a Chinstrap penguin.
- The coefficient $\beta_{3}$ captures the mean shift due to being a Gentoo penguin.

There is no proper slope interpretation here because none of independent variables are continuous.
Nevertheless, this model illustrates how linear regression models averages, conditional on the predictors.

## The Model Fit

We use the `statsmodels` package to fit a regression model using the formula interface, similar to R's interface.
It's good practice to summarize the fit of any model; a standard way of doing this for linear regression is to construct a regression table.

```{python}
#| echo: false
model = (
  smf.ols(
    "body_mass_g ~ C(sex, Treatment(reference='female'))"
    " + C(species, Treatment(reference='Adelie'))",
    data = penguins
  )
  .fit()
)

# The model boject contains information for a regression table.
regtable = pd.DataFrame({
  "Estimate": model.params,
  "Std. Error": model.bse,
  "t": model.tvalues,
  "p-value": model.pvalues,
})

# We change the labels of each coefficient to make them human-readable.
regtable.index = ["Intercept", "Is Male", "Is Chinstrap", "Is Gentoo"]
regtable
```

- The fitted `model` object in the code stores all the information we need. It was used to create this plot.
- The standard errors can be used to construct confidence intervals around our estimates $\beta_{j}$.
- The $t$-statistics are associated with hypothesis tests. Specifically, we use them to assess whether each $\beta_{j} = 0$ (null hypothesis). That is, we test each coefficient one at a time.
- In practice, we should adjust the $p$-values due to our *multiple comparisons*.

## Visualization

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false
# Fitted body mass for every combination of species and sex.
# We use this to show the regression fit.
species_order = ["Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"]
sex_order = ["female", "male"]
fitted = pd.DataFrame(
  list(itertools.product(species_order, sex_order)),
  columns=["species", "sex"],
)
fitted["predicted"] = model.predict(fitted)

# Set color options and offsets; here dodge = True places each sex
colors = {"female": "#2a78d6", "male": "#eb6834"}
offsets = {"female": -0.2, "male": 0.2}

# Observed penguins
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.stripplot(
  data = penguins,
  x = "species",
  y = "body_mass_g",
  hue = "sex",
  order = species_order,
  hue_order = sex_order,
  palette = colors,
  dodge = True,
  jitter = 0.12,
  alpha = 0.45,
  size = 4,
  ax = ax,
)

# Fitted values from the model
for i, species in enumerate(species_order):
  for sex in sex_order:
    row = fitted[(fitted["species"] == species) & (fitted["sex"] == sex)]
    x = i + offsets[sex]
    y = row["predicted"].iloc[0]
    ax.hlines(y, x - 0.15, x + 0.15, color="black", linewidth=2)

ax.set_xlabel("Species")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
ax.set_title("Body mass by species and sex (fitted values in black)")
ax.legend(title = "Sex", frameon = False)
sns.despine(ax = ax)

plt.show()
```

- The reference group are female Adelie penguins.
- Changing each categorical variable, `species` or `sex`, yields a change in the mean.
- Adelie and Chinstrap penguins have similar body masses. This explains why `"Is Chinstrap"` has little effect (small coefficient) and relatively large $p$-value.

## Issues

- In the EDA page, `female` was mapped to orange and `male` was mapped to blue. Here the colors are switched.
- Our Quarto pages have to reload nearly the same packages in each case.
- Some of the plots are long. Editing some of the options/settings is fragile because we hardcoded some values instead of using variables.
- What if we chose to analyze a different regression, or we added a continuous variable to the model? The regression table code would have to change in a few places.

The fix for most of these problems (and possibly others not listed here) is to **put most of the project code inside functions**.
